title: Hex vs Sigma vs Omni (2026): pricing, AI, semantic models, and governance for growth-stage data teams
summary: Hex is notebook-first with published per-editor prices, Sigma is a spreadsheet on your warehouse, and Omni is a governed semantic model. Here's how they…
body_markdown:
Hex, Sigma, and Omni answer different questions. Hex is the pick when your analysts live in SQL and Python notebooks and publish apps for everyone else. Sigma is the pick when business users think in spreadsheets and you want them working directly on Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks. Omni is the pick when you want one governed semantic model, managed in Git, behind every dashboard and AI answer. As of November 2026, only Hex publishes prices; Sigma and Omni are quote-only, and all three now charge credits for AI.


Everything below was checked against each vendor’s official pricing pages and documentation on November 20, 2026. For two-way comparisons, see[Hex vs Sigma](https://www.basedash.com/vs/hex-vs-sigma) ,[Hex vs Omni](https://www.basedash.com/vs/hex-vs-omni) , and[Omni vs Sigma](https://www.basedash.com/vs/omni-vs-sigma) . If you are leaving Hex entirely, our[Hex alternatives guide](https://www.basedash.com/blog/hex-alternatives-2026-modern-bi-tools-compared) covers a wider set.

## How we compared Hex, Sigma, and Omni


The criteria come from the questions growth-stage teams ask when these three share a shortlist:


1. **Cost at 15 to 40 people.** What is published, which seats are paid, and how AI is metered.
2. **Self-serve and setup.** Can someone who doesn’t write SQL build or ask without a data engineer?
3. **Semantic modeling.** Where metric definitions live, and whether they work with dbt and Git.
4. **Governance.** Row-level security, SSO protocol, SCIM, and audit logs.
5. **AI features.** Natural language querying, AI building, and MCP access.


## What do Hex, Sigma, and Omni cost for a growth-stage team?


**Hex** is the only one of the three with list prices. Community is free, Professional is $36 per editor per month, Team is $75 per editor per month, and Enterprise is custom ([Hex pricing](https://hex.tech/pricing/) ). Every plan allows unlimited users, but seat type matters. Editors build notebooks and apps; viewers open apps and shared Threads, and viewer seats “may be free or paid depending on your pricing plan” ([Hex roles](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/collaborate/sharing-and-permissions/roles) ). Asking questions in Threads or using Explore needs an Explorer role or higher, a per-seat add-on on Team and Enterprise priced through sales. AI runs on credits: 30 a month per Professional editor, 40 per Team editor, 10 per Team Explorer, with 50-credit top-ups for $25 ([Hex credits](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/administration/credits) ).


For a 25-person team with five editors on Team, the published part is $375 a month; the rest depends on how many of the other 20 need Explorer seats.


**Sigma** doesn’t publish prices; its pricing URL redirects to a contact form, and the[license overview](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/account-type-and-license-overview) tells buyers to contact their account executive. Licenses are tiered by what people do: View, Act (forms and input tables), Analyze (ad hoc analysis), and Build (create and share workbooks). Since November 1, 2026, each message sent to a Sigma agent costs 0.1 credit, and the credit price is also quote-only ([billable usage events](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/about-billable-usage-events) ).


**Omni** doesn’t publish prices either; there is no public pricing page, and trials start from a[request form](https://omni.co/demo) . Each account gets an included AI allotment, pooled across the account, and usage beyond it is “billed at $1.00 per credit” once an admin enables overage ([Omni AI usage](https://docs.omni.co/ai/settings/usage) ).


None of the three is purely usage-based: Hex and Sigma charge by seat type, Omni by negotiated contract, and all three meter AI on top. Our[BI pricing breakdown](https://www.basedash.com/blog/bi-tool-pricing-plans-seat-limits-and-ai-costs-2026) compares seat limits and AI costs across more tools.


## Which is easiest for non-technical users: Hex, Sigma, or Omni?


**Sigma** is the most familiar for spreadsheet users. Workbooks look and behave like a spreadsheet over live warehouse tables, input tables let people add their own rows, and Sigma Assistant is a “natural language query (NLQ) interface” for asking questions in plain English ([Sigma Assistant](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/ask-natural-language-queries-with-assistant) ). In October 2026, Assistant in the workbook became generally available for building and editing dashboards too.


**Omni** gives three ways in: natural language, a visual point-and-click interface, or SQL ([Omni querying](https://docs.omni.co/analyze-explore/querying) ). Spreadsheet tabs offer Excel-style calculations on live data. Because every query runs through the shared model, business users pick from curated fields instead of raw tables.


**Hex** is built for people who write code. Non-technical users mostly consume published apps, and Hex’s self-serve tools, Threads for chat and Explore for drag-and-drop drill-down, need an Explorer seat. Explore from an app or a data object is a Team and Enterprise feature ([Hex Explore](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/share-insights/explore) ).


Setup effort follows the same pattern. All three query the warehouse live, so none needs an extract pipeline. Sigma needs the least before business users get value: connect the warehouse and they can start on lightly modeled tables. Omni starts from a schema model that mirrors your database, but self-serve and AI quality depend on someone curating topics and fields. Hex is fastest for an analyst who writes SQL and slowest for everyone else, who need published apps or semantic models first.


For a team without a dedicated data engineer, Sigma and Omni are easier for business users than Hex. Sigma wins for people who already think in spreadsheets; Omni wins once someone has curated the model.


## How do Hex, Sigma, and Omni handle semantic models and dbt?


**Omni** puts the semantic layer at the center: a schema model that mirrors the database, a shared governed model, and workbook models, where “changes you make in a workbook land in the workbook model first” until someone promotes them ([model promotion](https://docs.omni.co/modeling/develop/promotion) ). The model lives in YAML, can require Git pull requests ([Omni Git](https://docs.omni.co/integrations/git) ), and the dbt integration is bi-directional: it reads dbt metadata and the dbt Semantic Layer and pushes descriptions and exposures back ([Omni dbt](https://docs.omni.co/integrations/dbt) ). The Modeling Agent, announced in April 2026, drafts views, relationships, dimensions, and measures from your tables.


**Sigma** uses data models with reusable metrics and defined relationships. Since April 2026, data models can be managed as JSON or YAML through an API, and in November 2026 workbooks and reports followed ([data models as code](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/manage-data-models-as-code) ). Sigma reads the dbt Semantic Layer, but “the dbt Semantic Layer is not available for dbt Core integrations,” so you need dbt Cloud ([dbt Semantic Layer in Sigma](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/configure-a-dbt-semantic-layer-integration) ). Sigma doesn’t document a native Git integration; the as-code API is the path to CI/CD.


**Hex** added semantic models on Team and Enterprise. You can author them in Hex’s Modeling Workbench or import them with Semantic Model Sync, which is in beta and supports dbt MetricFlow, Cube, and Snowflake semantic views ([semantic model sync](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/connect-to-data/semantic-models/semantic-model-sync/intro) ). The dbt path imports MetricFlow YAML rather than querying the live dbt Semantic Layer. Git support is a one-way export of projects to GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket on Team and Enterprise ([Hex Git export](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/explore-data/projects/git-export) ).


For a Series B team on Snowflake that wants semantic modeling plus collaboration, Omni has the most complete model and Sigma the closest thing to spreadsheet collaboration. Our comparison of[BI tools with built-in semantic layers](https://www.basedash.com/blog/best-bi-tools-with-built-in-semantic-layers-compared-2026) covers this in more depth.


## Which has stronger governance: row-level security, SSO, and SCIM?


**Omni** enforces row-level security in the model. Access filters limit “access to rows in a dataset based on user attributes,” and access grants restrict individual fields ([access filters](https://docs.omni.co/modeling/topics/parameters/access-filters) ). It supports SAML and OIDC, SCIM through Okta, Microsoft Entra, and Rippling, and audit logs delivered to S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage ([audit logs](https://docs.omni.co/administration/audit-logs) ).


**Sigma** enforces row-level security with formulas such as` CurrentUserAttributeText("Region") = \[Store Region\]` ([row-level security](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/set-up-row-level-security) ) and offers column-level masking in data models. It supports SAML 2.0 and OIDC. SCIM requires the organization to use SAML ([Sigma SCIM](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/manage-users-and-teams-with-scim) ). Audit logging is off by default and must be enabled by Sigma support.


**Hex** has the narrowest set. Single sign-on is “via OpenID Connect (OIDC). SAML is not supported,” and it is an Enterprise feature ([Hex SSO](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/administration/sso) ). Directory sync for Okta, Rippling, Google, and Azure, audit logs, and OAuth data connections are Enterprise too. Row-level security for workspace users comes from the warehouse: OAuth connections “run each query under a user’s warehouse identity,” and they work with Snowflake, Databricks, and BigQuery ([OAuth connections](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/connect-to-data/data-connections/oauth-data-connections) ). Hex-native row filtering is documented for signed embedding, not for internal users.


For a fintech or other regulated team on BigQuery that needs strong governance, Omni and Sigma both cover SAML, SCIM, and in-tool row-level security. Hex works if your identity provider supports OIDC and you are comfortable enforcing rows in BigQuery itself.


## Hex vs Sigma vs Omni AI features


**Omni Agent** answers questions, generates queries and charts, and builds dashboards ([Omni AI](https://docs.omni.co/ai) ). It is “enabled by default,” runs on Amazon Bedrock or Microsoft Foundry depending on your deployment, and accepts bring-your-own models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Vertex AI, Snowflake Cortex, and others ([LLM settings](https://docs.omni.co/ai/settings/llm-settings) ). Omni also has a Workbook Agent and an[MCP server](https://docs.omni.co/ai/mcp) that can scope queries to a user’s permissions.


**Sigma** made Sigma agents and Assistant in the workbook generally available in October 2026 ([Sigma release notes](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/changelog/2026-10-02) ). AI runs either through a warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks) or an external provider such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or Bedrock, and Sigma’s docs note “you cannot choose which model Sigma uses” ([supported AI models](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/supported-ai-models) ). Sigma’s[MCP server](https://help.sigmacomputing.com/docs/use-sigma-mcp-server) lets Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and others search, query, and build workbooks.


**Hex** has the Hex agent and Notebook agent for analysts, Threads for conversational questions, Context Studio for curating what the agent knows, and a governed mode that limits the agent to endorsed sources. Hex’s own docs say governed mode “isn’t a hard security boundary” ([governed mode](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/agent-management/governed-mode) ). Its[MCP server](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/api-integrations/mcp-server) is on Team and Enterprise, and[Hex 4.0](https://hex.tech/blog/introducing-hex-4-0) , in public beta since October 2026, backs projects with code files.


For AI answers to business users without a full-time data engineer, Omni’s model-grounded agent and Sigma’s Assistant need less setup than Hex’s Threads, which also needs Explorer seats.


## Hex vs Omni for notebook exploration plus governed dashboards


Hex is the better notebook: multiplayer editing with cell locking ([real-time collaboration](https://learn.hex.tech/docs/collaborate/real-time-collaboration) ), SQL and Python in one project, and in-memory DuckDB for querying dataframes. Omni is the better governed dashboard layer, because every dashboard and agent answer inherits the same model and access filters. Some teams run both, Hex for the analytics team’s deep work and Omni for company-wide dashboards. If you can only buy one, choose by who your main users are.


## When Basedash fits instead


If your team is small, has no data engineer, and wants AI to do most of the building, Basedash is a different shape worth comparing: people ask questions in chat and the[AI data analyst](https://www.basedash.com/features/ai-data-analyst) writes the SQL, builds charts, and assembles dashboards.


**Basedash fact card (verified November 20, 2026)**


- **Pricing:** Startup is $1,000 per month plus AI usage for up to 25 users, with $1,000 a month in AI credits included; Enterprise is custom ([pricing](https://www.basedash.com/pricing) ,[plan details](https://www.basedash.com/docs/administration/pricing) ).
- **Free trial:** 14 days, no card. No free plan.
- **Deployment:** Cloud, or[self-hosted](https://www.basedash.com/features/self-hosting) on Enterprise.
- **Databases:** Live queries on Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, ClickHouse, Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, and more, plus 750+ SaaS sources synced into the[Basedash Warehouse](https://www.basedash.com/features/warehouse) ([data sources](https://www.basedash.com/docs/data-sources/introduction) ).
- **Semantic layer:**[Models](https://www.basedash.com/features/models) with SQL, measures, segments, version history, and admin verification; the AI can create and update them. No Git integration.
- **Row-level security:** Postgres and Supabase only, through a` basedash.groups` session variable ([row-level security](https://www.basedash.com/docs/administration/row-level-security) ). Schema, table, and column access rules hide data from the AI on any source.
- **SSO and SCIM:** SAML 2.0 or OIDC, plus SCIM, on Enterprise ([SSO](https://www.basedash.com/docs/administration/sso) ).
- **AI and MCP:** Chat, AI-built dashboards, scheduled insights, and automations on every plan, plus an[MCP server](https://www.basedash.com/features/mcp-server) .
- **Embedding:** Enterprise only, through an iframe or the` @basedash/embed` React SDK.
- **Best for:** Teams of up to 25 who want AI to handle the SQL and dashboard building.
- **Not ideal for:** Notebook-heavy analyst work (Hex), spreadsheet modeling on the warehouse (Sigma), or a Git-managed semantic model with warehouse-wide row-level security (Omni).


## Which should you choose?


- **Analytics team that writes SQL and Python:** Hex. It has the best notebook and the only published price, but budget for Explorer seats if business users need to ask questions.
- **Moving off Hex because of cost, 25 people on Snowflake, non-technical stakeholders:** Sigma if those stakeholders live in spreadsheets; Omni if you have someone to own a semantic model. Get quotes from both, since neither publishes prices.
- **15-person fintech data team on BigQuery that needs governance and natural language:** Omni or Sigma. Both support SAML, SCIM, and in-tool row-level security. Hex lacks SAML and relies on BigQuery for row-level security.
- **40-person analytics team:** Omni for a shared model across many builders, or Hex if most of the 40 write code.
- **Series B on Snowflake wanting semantic modeling and collaboration:** Omni for Git-managed modeling, Sigma for live co-editing in workbooks.
- **No data engineer, mostly business users, AI-first:** Sigma or Omni among the three, or Basedash if you want AI to do the building.


## Frequently asked questions


### Is Hex cheaper than Sigma or Omni?


Hex is the only one with published prices: Professional costs $36 and Team $75 per editor per month as of November 2026, so a few editors and many viewers can be inexpensive. Costs rise when business users need Explorer seats to ask questions in Threads or use Explore, since Explorer is a sales-priced add-on. Sigma and Omni are quote-only, so a direct comparison needs real quotes. All three meter AI separately: Hex sells 50 credits for $25, Sigma charges 0.1 credit per agent message, and Omni bills $1.00 per credit over its included allotment.


### Which is better for non-technical users, Hex or Sigma?


Sigma is better for non-technical users. Its workbooks work like a spreadsheet on live warehouse data, and Sigma Assistant answers natural language questions. Hex is built around SQL and Python notebooks; non-technical users mostly view published apps, and asking questions in Threads or drilling down with Explore requires an Explorer seat, which is an add-on on Team and Enterprise. Hex suits teams where a few analysts build and everyone else consumes. Sigma suits teams where business users want to build their own analysis.


### Does Hex support SAML SSO?


No. As of November 2026, Hex’s documentation says it supports single sign-on through OpenID Connect (OIDC) and that SAML is not supported. SSO is on the Enterprise plan, along with directory sync for Okta, Rippling, Google, and Azure. Most major identity providers support OIDC, so this is rarely a blocker, but check with your IT team if your security policy requires SAML. Sigma and Omni both support SAML and OIDC.


### Which has the better semantic layer, Omni or Sigma?


Omni’s semantic layer is more central and more developer-friendly. Every query runs through a shared YAML model that can be managed in Git with pull requests, and its dbt integration both reads dbt metadata and the dbt Semantic Layer and writes back. Sigma’s data models define metrics and relationships and can be managed as JSON or YAML through an API, but Git is not native, and its dbt Semantic Layer support requires dbt Cloud. Pick Omni if consistent metric definitions matter most; pick Sigma if spreadsheet flexibility matters more.


### Can Hex, Sigma, and Omni connect to BigQuery and Snowflake?


Yes. All three connect live to Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift, and Postgres, along with others such as ClickHouse and MotherDuck (both in beta on Sigma). The differences are in governance. Hex can run queries under each user’s own Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks identity through OAuth connections on Enterprise. Sigma can assign warehouse roles from user attributes and enforce row-level security with formulas. Omni applies access filters from its model to every query.


### What should a startup data team choose between Hex and Omni?


Choose by who the main users are. If the data team is two to five analysts who write SQL and Python and publish results, Hex is the better fit and its pricing is published. If the goal is to let the rest of the company self-serve from consistent definitions, Omni is the better fit, because its shared model and access filters apply to every dashboard and AI answer. Some startups begin with Hex for analysis and add Omni or Sigma once business users need their own dashboards.
